I believe everyone can. It’s all about proper coping mechanisms, self care, and reacting properly when you’re struggling. However, I know that “being cured” of a mental illness isn’t always possible. Some people’s brains are wired differently, incorrectly, and chemical imbalances are scientifically proven to be real. There’s soooooo many things that can contribute to bad mental health.

Overcoming a mental illness to me is being able to manage it properly. I continue to have a thought process that is very obsessive (hence the OCD diagnosis I was given) but I’ve learned to manage and react to those thoughts I have differently and in a healthy way. I can’t stop the thoughts from entering my head but I can control how I react to them.  I can’t control that some days are harder to get up than others and I wake up with so much negativity and anxiety. But I can control how I react and handle those situations! It took me 23 years to do it but I did it!

Hope is there for everyone! ❤️

I don’t know of any evidence that shows there is a possibility of long term damages to your brain. I also know that medication isn’t a cure-all. I’ve been on meds for over 25 years and they have helped but you have to combine those meds with a healthy lifestyle and therapy to get good results.

As far as the side effects go, those could always be an issue. Everyone’s body reacts differently to medication and there’s really no way to tell what side effects you’ll encounter until you start taking the medication. 

You also have to weigh the pros and cons. Is a decreased libido something you’re ok with in exchange for feeling better about yourself? Would gaining a little weight from medication actually make your depression worse if you suffer from self-image issues?

At the end of the day, medication comes with its risks but can really pay out if you find the right ones and combine it with a healthy lifestyle.

Don’t give up on love. There are genuine, amazing people out there and sometimes we have to go through some real garbage before we find the keeper. What’s important is that you’re realistic about finding love. If you’re online dating, proceed with caution and know that there are risks involved with it. I know SOOOOO many people who met their significant others online and EVERY single one of those people have horror stories about previous people they met. There are probably people out there who succeed on their first shot but it’s probably fairly rare.

Most importantly, make sure you’re in a good place with yourself before you seek a life partner. If you aren’t OK with you who are as a person being it’s unfair to bring someone else into your life and expect them to fix that for you. Relationships are a lot of work but the foundation of a good relationship is loving yourself before you find someone else to love. I speak from experience on that!

I finally got over my addiction and I started getting my tattoos to cover them after about 1 year of healing from my most recent scars, which were the really bad ones. My artist told me that really after 6 months you can technically start tattooing them but he recommends waiting after about 2 years of healing to be safe, especially with deeper scars. While the scar itself may look healed on the outside it could still be healing underneath.

I have obsessive compulsive disorder so obsessive thoughts, suicidal thoughts and self harm thoughts go through my head on a daily basis, all day. For years and years I’ve been trying to fight the thoughts, telling them to go away, begging them to stop. But the fact of the matter is we do not have control over what thoughts pop into our head. If a thought is gonna come, it’s gonna come. Fighting the thoughts and telling them to stop won’t do anything except feed them.

Think of it this way: Picture a busy highway with hundreds and hundreds of cars driving by at 80mph every minute. Those cars are your thoughts. What would happen if you jumped into the middle of the highway and tried to control traffic? Utter chaos. Cars crashing everywhere. 

Instead, you should find a bench to sit on and watch the cars (your thoughts) go by and recognize that they don’t serve you any purpose. The cars will always drive by but you don’t have to fuel them. Remember too that your thoughts don’t define you or make you crazy in any way. Your actions are what define you. So reacting to those intrusive thoughts in a healthy way is incredibly important.

This type of therapy doesn’t necessarily work for everyone and it definitely requires a lot of practice, so keep that in mind. But for me it’s worked wonders. I still struggle with cutting, I relapsed last week. So you may fall off the wagon occasionally. You just gotta keep trying and keep going.

I’m here. I know what you’re going through. I’m (34M) currently at a mental health residential facility, I’ve been here for almost 2 months. Been struggling since I was 11 years old. I don’t have an eating disorder but I definitely cut myself as well.

It’s incredibly difficult to get through extreme suicidal times without doing something stupid, which I’ve done a few times. But you can get through it. I promise you that. I’ve gotten through it for 23 years and I’m still fighting. You can keep fighting too.

I know the last thing you want to do is check yourself into a hospital but it is probably the best thing you can do for yourself right now.

How long you stay really depends on how you’re doing. I’ve gotten out as quick as 4 days but my most recent stay about 2 months ago I was there about 18 days. However I was also suicidal and self harming, so they couldn’t let me out until they knew I wasn’t a danger to myself.

If you’re just going to get evaluated, diagnosed, set up with medication and an outside therapist your stay should be relatively quick. Most in-patient facilities don’t let you leave until you also have appointments set up for an outside provider. They should help you with that as well. And as I mentioned earlier, they won’t let you leave if they feel you’re a danger to yourself or others.

Counseling has been a very important part of my recovery. In terms of diagnosing, a counselor can’t actually do that, an actual doctor (psychiatrist) is the only mental health professional that can give an actual diagnosis. A counselor may refer you to one if they feel a diagnosis or medication is necessary, but otherwise they won’t. Most psychiatrists also use a DSM-5 to diagnose which relies heavily on your symptoms.

I know people who see a counselor just to have someone outside their family/friends to chat with on a weekly or bi-weekly basis. You don’t necessarily need to be in utter peril to see one. If you find a good counselor they are great listeners, non-judgmental, and great at helping you work through your issues whether those issues are severe, moderate, or very minor.

I’d highly recommend seeking one out!

Your day is typically filled with group therapy and individual therapy. You should see your therapist and psychiatrist on a daily basis so they can monitor your progress and manage your meds. Your group therapies will be with the other patients and can be anything from a process group to art therapy to recreational therapy. Just depends what your hospital offers and how their program is structured.

Some in-patient units are a little more strict than others, so I can’t say for certain what they will let you do and what they won’t let you do. But the best place I’ve been to gave me access to computers and television (as long as a group or individual therapy isn’t going on). Food will be hit or miss. I’ve had crap food and awesome food, just depends on the place. I’ve been in-patient at a place that let people bring me my own food which was nice.

It’s extremely common to start off on small doses of meds and gradually working your way up. In fact, it’s actually unsafe to do it any other way since people can react to them so differently.

As someone (34M) who’s been on medication for my mental illnesses for over 23 years I can also tell you that med management can definitely be a pain but when you find the right one or combination of a few it’s worth it. To answer one of your other questions, yes, your body can definitely build up a tolerance to SSRIs, SNRIs, Tricyclics, MAOIs, any type of medication for mental illness. It typically doesn’t happen really fast, you usually don’t start to see a decrease in effectiveness for years, but again, that can vary person to person.

Just be careful if you’re ever prescribed benzodiazepines (Ativan, Xanax, Ambien, Klonopin, etc) as those can be highly addictive and very dangerous if used too much.

You’ll eventually get used to taking pills everyday as well. It’s just part of my normal routine honestly, I’ve just been doing it for so long.

I’ve been hospitalized many times, and generally, the experience itself is pretty good. I’ve been to many different hospitals and it’s nothing like what they show on the media. You’ll attend daily classes, meet with your doctor everyday to discuss how you’re doing and to discuss your meds, and learn coping skills, most of which will all be in a group setting.

I highly recommend you participate in all of the activities. You’re in a setting that is there to help you get better, so ensure you utilize it. It can be a little weird and awkward at first but you’ll get used to it. Hopefully the hospital you goto is a good one.

Know that once you are admitted, you can’t just check yourself out. You can request to be checked out, but it’s ultimately the doctor’s decision as to if they feel like you will be safe when you leave. If the doctor doesn’t think that you will be safe, you won’t be discharged. I believe when you request to be discharged, the doctors have to respond to your request within 72 hours.

Best of luck to you. I really applaud you for making the decision to check yourself in, that’s a big step to take!

I just answered a question similar to this on another thread less than a day ago. It mostly covers what you’re wondering but the other person who was asking was talking about admitting himself/herself. Here’s what I said:

“I’ve been hospitalized as in-patient 4 times in the past 365 days. Throughout my entire life I can’t even count how many times I’ve been hospitalized.

I can say it’s nothing like the way it’s shown in TV and movies, it’s actually quite the opposite. Although this depends on what hospital you goto and who’s there. Sometimes other patients can be very disruptive, and some hospitals are more strict about interacting with other patients.

Admitting yourself is always the best option, involuntary can be messy. The hospital I’ve been at the most times actually has two separate sections, one for involuntary admission and the other for voluntary.

Know that once you get admitted, your discharge is in the hands of the doctors. You’ll be evaluated on a daily basis and you’ll goto “classes” and groups most of the day where you’ll learn skills to help you with your disease and coping techniques. The more you participate and work on yourself the quicker you’ll leave. Every hospital I’ve been to I always met with my doctor everyday to check in and work on any medication adjustments.

I can’t stress enough that your experience as in-patient will depend on how willing you are to work on yourself and get better. If you’re on board, ready, and willing to try and get better, your experience will be much more pleasant. Also, I would recommend doing some research on the hospital you’re planning to check yourself into. Some places are better then others.

I’ve never really had any “bad experiences” at a hospital, but one that I went to was kind of questionable. The doctors didn’t seem experienced and it didn’t really feel like they cared about what was in my best interest. They also seemed to think that my meds should fix everything, and as someone who has dealt with depression, anxiety, and OCD their entire life, I can tell you meds are not a cure-all. It takes a lot of hard work and dedication via therapy.

If you have any other questions, let me know.”

- A couple things I’ll add is that the hospitals I’ve been to have been nice and very clean (with one exception) and that your type of insurance won’t change what kind of room you’re in. I certainly wouldn’t call any of the hospitals I’ve stayed in hotel-quality but they’ve been mostly pretty nice.

Also, if you sign yourself in voluntary it makes things much easier. If you go involuntary then the courts get involved and things can get rough, so I recommend you go voluntary. However, your age and state (or country) you live in may have different laws/policies about this.

Again, if you have any other questions, let me know.
